stem.en: Which of the following is a benzylic halide?

explanation.en: In C₆H₅CH₂Cl the halogen is on an sp³ carbon attached to the benzene ring: a benzylic halide. C₆H₅Cl is an aryl halide, CH₂=CHCl vinylic and CH₂=CHCH₂Cl allylic.

stem.en: The IUPAC name of (CH₃)₃CBr is:

explanation.en: The longest chain has three carbons; C-2 carries both Br and a methyl group: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (common name tert-butyl bromide).

stem.en: Which carbon–halogen bond is the longest?

explanation.en: Bond length grows with the size of the halogen: C–F 139 pm < C–Cl 178 pm < C–Br 193 pm < C–I 214 pm.

stem.en: Among CH₃F, CH₃Cl, CH₃Br and CH₃I, the largest dipole moment is shown by:

explanation.en: Dipole moment = charge × distance. F is most electronegative but the C–F bond is very short, so CH₃Cl (1.860 D) edges out CH₃F (1.847 D); then CH₃Br (1.830 D) and CH₃I (1.636 D).

solution.en: F is most electronegative but the C–F bond is very short, so CH₃Cl (1.860 D) edges out CH₃F (1.847 D); then CH₃Br (1.830 D) and CH₃I (1.636 D).

stem.en: How many structural (constitutional) isomers are possible for C₄H₉Br?

explanation.en: 1-Bromobutane, 2-bromobutane, 1-bromo-2-methylpropane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane: four. (2-Bromobutane also has two enantiomers, but those are stereoisomers.)

stem.en: Which reagent converts ethanol to chloroethane with both by-products escaping as gases?

explanation.en: C₂H₅OH + SOCl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + SO₂↑ + HCl↑. Both by-products are gases, so pure chloroethane is left behind.

stem.en: The reaction CH₃CH₂Br + NaI → CH₃CH₂I + NaBr in dry acetone is called the:

explanation.en: Finkelstein reaction: halogen exchange with NaI in dry acetone. NaBr does not dissolve in acetone and precipitates, driving the reaction forward.

stem.en: Which has the highest boiling point?

explanation.en: For the same alkyl group, boiling point rises with molar mass and van der Waals forces: RI > RBr > RCl > RF.

stem.en: Propene reacts with HBr in the presence of benzoyl peroxide to give mainly:

explanation.en: Peroxide effect (Kharasch): HBr adds by a free-radical path against Markovnikov’s rule, so Br goes to the terminal carbon: 1-bromopropane.

solution.en: Peroxide effect (Kharasch): HBr adds by a free-radical path against Markovnikov’s rule, so Br goes to the terminal carbon: 1-bromopropane.

stem.en: Among the dichlorobenzenes, the highest melting point is shown by:

explanation.en: The para isomer is symmetrical and packs best in the crystal lattice, so it melts highest (about 323 K, against 256 K for ortho and 249 K for meta).

stem.en: Which alkyl bromide reacts fastest by the SN2 mechanism?

explanation.en: SN2 needs backside attack; bulky groups block it. Reactivity: CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3°.

stem.en: The rate of an SN1 reaction depends on:

options.en: The concentration of the nucleophile only
The concentration of the alkyl halide only

explanation.en: In SN1 the slow step is ionisation of R–X into a carbocation; the nucleophile joins later in a fast step. Rate = k[R–X].

stem.en: An alkyl halide reacts with AgCN to give mainly:

explanation.en: AgCN is mainly covalent, so the Ag–C bond is not free; the nitrogen lone pair attacks, giving R–NC (isocyanide). Ionic KCN attacks through carbon, giving R–CN.

stem.en: Which of the following undergoes SN1 reaction fastest?

explanation.en: SN1 speed follows carbocation stability. (C₆H₅)₂CH⁺ is stabilised by resonance with two benzene rings, more than C₆H₅CH₂⁺ with one; primary and methyl cations are very unstable.

solution.en: (C₆H₅)₂CH⁺ is stabilised by resonance with two benzene rings, more than C₆H₅CH₂⁺ with one; primary and methyl cations are very unstable.

stem.en: For an SN2 reaction, rate = k[RX][OH⁻]. If [RX] is halved and [OH⁻] is doubled, the rate:

explanation.en: New rate = k(½[RX])(2[OH⁻]) = k[RX][OH⁻]: unchanged.

stem.en: A racemic mixture is optically inactive because of:

options.en: A plane of symmetry in each molecule

explanation.en: A racemic mixture has equal amounts of the d and l enantiomers; their opposite rotations cancel. This is external compensation. Internal compensation is the meso case.

stem.en: The major product when 2-bromobutane is heated with alcoholic KOH is:

explanation.en: Alcoholic KOH causes β-elimination. By Zaitsev’s rule the more substituted alkene, but-2-ene, is the major product (about 80%).

stem.en: Which of these molecules is chiral?

explanation.en: In 2-bromobutane C-2 carries four different groups: H, Br, CH₃ and C₂H₅. In the others, at least two groups on each carbon are identical.

stem.en: A mixture of CH₃Br and C₂H₅Br is treated with sodium in dry ether. The product is:

options.en: A mixture of ethane, propane and butane

explanation.en: Wurtz coupling joins any two alkyl groups at random: CH₃–CH₃ (ethane), CH₃–C₂H₅ (propane) and C₂H₅–C₂H₅ (butane). This is why Wurtz is used with one halide only.

solution.en: Wurtz coupling joins any two alkyl groups at random: CH₃–CH₃ (ethane), CH₃–C₂H₅ (propane) and C₂H₅–C₂H₅ (butane).
This is why Wurtz is used with one halide only.

stem.en: Grignard reagents must be prepared in dry ether because with water they:

explanation.en: R–MgX is a very strong base: R–MgX + H₂O → R–H + Mg(OH)X. Even traces of moisture destroy it, giving the alkane.

stem.en: Chlorobenzene is converted to phenol by heating with aqueous NaOH at:

explanation.en: Aryl halides resist nucleophilic substitution, so chlorobenzene needs NaOH at 623 K and 300 atm, followed by acidification, to give phenol.

stem.en: Haloarenes are less reactive than haloalkanes towards nucleophilic substitution mainly because:

options.en: The C–X bond has partial double-bond character due to resonance
Halogens are less electronegative in arenes

explanation.en: The halogen lone pair is delocalised into the ring, giving the C–X bond partial double-bond character. The sp² carbon also makes the bond shorter and stronger, and the phenyl cation is unstable.

stem.en: C₆H₅Cl + CH₃Cl + 2Na (dry ether) gives:

explanation.en: Wurtz–Fittig reaction joins an aryl and an alkyl group: C₆H₅–CH₃, toluene.

stem.en: Which compound undergoes nucleophilic substitution by OH⁻ most easily?

explanation.en: Nitro groups at ortho and para positions withdraw electrons and stabilise the carbanion intermediate. With three of them, 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene is hydrolysed by warm water.

solution.en: Nitro groups at ortho and para positions withdraw electrons and stabilise the carbanion intermediate.
With three of them, 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene is hydrolysed by warm water.

stem.en: Chlorobenzene reacts with Cl₂ in the presence of anhydrous FeCl₃. The major product is:

explanation.en: Cl is an ortho/para director (lone-pair resonance), though deactivating. Para is less crowded, so 1,4-dichlorobenzene is the major product.

stem.en:
Assertion (A): 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane undergoes S_N1 hydrolysis much faster than 1-bromobutane.
Reason (R): A tertiary carbocation is much more stable than a primary carbocation.

options.en: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation.en: The rate-determining step in S_N1 is carbocation formation; the stable 3° carbocation from 2-bromo-2-methylpropane forms readily. R explains A.

stem.en:
Assertion (A): Chlorobenzene undergoes electrophilic substitution mainly at the ortho and para positions.
Reason (R): Chlorine is a strongly activating group on the benzene ring.

options.en: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation.en: Chlorine deactivates the ring (−I effect) but directs ortho/para (+R effect raises electron density at o- and p-positions). A is true; R is false.

passage.en: A student compares the reactivity of three bromides. With sodium iodide in dry acetone, 1-bromobutane gives a precipitate of NaBr in about 2 minutes, 2-bromobutane takes about 10 minutes, and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane gives no precipitate even after an hour. She then repeats the experiment with silver nitrate in ethanol, a polar solvent in which the halide ion can leave first, and watches for a precipitate of AgBr.

stem.en: Why does 2-bromo-2-methylpropane react slowest with NaI in acetone?

options.en: Its C–Br bond is the strongest of the three
Bulky methyl groups block the back-side attack of I⁻ needed in S_N2

explanation.en: NaI in acetone is an S_N2 test. The nucleophile must attack from the side opposite the leaving group; three methyl groups around the carbon hinder this, so the reaction almost stops.

passage.en: A student compares the reactivity of three bromides. With sodium iodide in dry acetone, 1-bromobutane gives a precipitate of NaBr in about 2 minutes, 2-bromobutane takes about 10 minutes, and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane gives no precipitate even after an hour. She then repeats the experiment with silver nitrate in ethanol, a polar solvent in which the halide ion can leave first, and watches for a precipitate of AgBr.

stem.en: In the silver nitrate–ethanol test, which bromide should give a precipitate of AgBr first?

options.en: All three at the same time

explanation.en: In this polar solvent the reaction goes by S_N1, whose rate depends on carbocation stability (3° > 2° > 1°), so the order is reversed and the tertiary bromide reacts first.

stem.en: Which of the following statements about the SN2 reaction of an alkyl halide are correct? One or more options may be correct.

options.en: Its rate depends on the concentrations of both the alkyl halide and the nucleophile
At a chiral carbon it gives inversion of configuration
It goes through a carbocation intermediate

explanation.en: SN2 is a one-step, second-order reaction (rate = k[RX][Nu⁻]) with backside attack, so it inverts configuration. Crowding slows it, so the order is CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3°, and there is no carbocation (that is SN1).

stem.en: Which of the following statements are correct? One or more options may be correct.

options.en: An SN1 reaction at a chiral carbon gives mainly a racemic mixture
2-Bromobutane with alcoholic KOH gives but-1-ene as the major product
A Grignard reagent reacts with water to give an alkane

explanation.en: SN2 inverts configuration; since OH takes the place (and priority) of Br, R becomes S. SN1 goes through a flat carbocation attacked from both faces: racemisation. Zaitsev’s rule makes but-2-ene the major alkene. RMgX + H₂O → RH + Mg(OH)X.

stem.en: A sample of 2-bromobutane shows a specific rotation of +9.2°, while pure (+)-2-bromobutane has +23.1°. What percentage of the sample is the (+) enantiomer? Give the answer to the nearest whole number.
How many isomers in all, counting stereoisomers, are possible for C₄H₉Br? Give an integer.

explanation.en: Structural isomers: 1-bromobutane, 2-bromobutane, 1-bromo-2-methylpropane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (4). Only 2-bromobutane has a chiral carbon, so it exists as two enantiomers: 4 + 1 = 5.

stem.en: The correct order of reactivity towards an SN2 reaction is:

explanation.en: In SN2 the nucleophile attacks from the back; every extra alkyl group crowds that side, so methyl reacts fastest and tertiary slowest.

solution.en: In SN2 the nucleophile attacks from the back; every extra alkyl group crowds that side, so methyl reacts fastest and tertiary slowest.

stem.en: An alkyl halide RX reacts with AgCN to give mainly:

explanation.en: AgCN is mainly covalent, so the carbon of cyanide is tied up and the nitrogen lone pair attacks: isocyanide. Ionic KCN attacks through carbon and gives the cyanide.

stem.en: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane is heated with alcoholic KOH. The major product is:

explanation.en: β-Elimination by Zaitsev’s rule gives the more substituted alkene, (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃ (trisubstituted), as the major product.

solution.en: β-Elimination by Zaitsev’s rule gives the more substituted alkene, (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃ (trisubstituted), as the major product.

stem.en: The IUPAC name of (CH₃)₃C–CH₂Cl (neopentyl chloride) is:

explanation.en: The longest chain containing the C–Cl carbon has three carbons; numbering from the CH₂Cl end gives Cl at C-1 and two methyls at C-2: 1-chloro-2,2-dimethylpropane. Numbering from the other end gives higher locants; the butane name miscounts the chain (only 5 C in total, arranged as a propane with two methyls).

stem.en: The best reagent for converting an alcohol into an alkyl chloride, because both by-products are gases that escape, is:

explanation.en: $\text{R–OH} + \text{SOCl}_2 \rightarrow \text{R–Cl} + \text{SO}_2\uparrow + \text{HCl}\uparrow$. Both by-products leave as gases, so pure R–Cl is left. PCl₅ leaves liquid POCl₃, PCl₃ leaves H₃PO₃, and Lucas reagent works well only for 2° and 3° alcohols.

stem.en: Alkyl iodides are conveniently made by heating alkyl chlorides or bromides with NaI in dry acetone. This is the:

explanation.en: Finkelstein reaction: $\text{R–X} + \text{NaI} \rightarrow \text{R–I} + \text{NaX}$ (X = Cl, Br). NaCl and NaBr are insoluble in dry acetone and precipitate, which drives the equilibrium forward (Le Chatelier). Swarts gives fluorides; Sandmeyer works on diazonium salts; Wurtz couples alkyl halides.

stem.en: In the Swarts reaction an alkyl chloride or bromide is heated with a metallic fluoride such as AgF, Hg₂F₂, CoF₂ or SbF₃. The product is:

explanation.en: Swarts reaction: $\text{CH}_3\text{Br} + \text{AgF} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{F} + \text{AgBr}$. It is the standard way to make alkyl fluorides, since direct fluorination is too violent.

stem.en: The order of reactivity of halogen acids with a given alcohol is:

explanation.en: The H–X bond gets weaker down the group (HI weakest), so HI is the strongest acid and I⁻ is a good nucleophile. Reactivity: HI > HBr > HCl. HCl is so slow with primary alcohols that anhydrous ZnCl₂ is needed.

stem.en: Which isomer of C₄H₉Br has the highest boiling point?

explanation.en: For isomeric haloalkanes, branching makes the molecule more compact, reducing surface area and van der Waals forces, so the boiling point falls. The straight-chain 1-bromobutane (≈ 375 K) is highest; the most branched 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (≈ 346 K) is lowest.

stem.en: Chloroform is stored in closed, dark-coloured bottles filled to the brim because in air and light it is oxidised to the poisonous gas:

explanation.en: $2\text{CHCl}_3 + \text{O}_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} 2\text{COCl}_2 + 2\text{HCl}$. Phosgene (carbonyl chloride) is extremely poisonous. Dark bottles cut out light and filling to the brim keeps out air.

stem.en: Bromomethane is heated with sodium metal in dry ether. The organic product is:

explanation.en: Wurtz reaction: $2\text{CH}_3\text{Br} + 2\text{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \text{CH}_3\text{–CH}_3 + 2\text{NaBr}$. Two alkyl groups join, so the product has twice the carbon number: ethane.

stem.en: Benzenediazonium chloride is treated with cuprous chloride in HCl to give chlorobenzene. This is the:

explanation.en: Sandmeyer reaction: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^- \xrightarrow{\text{CuCl/HCl}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl} + \text{N}_2$. When copper powder and HCl are used instead, it is called the Gattermann reaction (Gattermann–Koch is a formylation and does not apply).

stem.en: Freon-12, once widely used as a refrigerant and aerosol propellant, is:

explanation.en: Freon-12 is dichlorodifluoromethane, CCl₂F₂. Freons are stable, non-toxic and non-corrosive, but in the stratosphere UV light breaks C–Cl bonds and the Cl radicals destroy ozone.

stem.en: Methylmagnesium bromide reacts with water to give:

explanation.en: The C–Mg bond is highly polar with carbon carrying negative charge, so the Grignard reagent is a very strong base and takes a proton from water: $\text{CH}_3\text{MgBr} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_4 + \text{Mg(OH)Br}$. This is why Grignard reagents must be made and used in dry ether.

stem.en: How many structural isomers are possible for C₄H₉Br?

explanation.en: Two carbon skeletons (butane, 2-methylpropane), each with two distinct positions: 1-bromobutane, 2-bromobutane, 1-bromo-2-methylpropane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, so 4. (2-Bromobutane is chiral, but enantiomers are stereoisomers, not structural isomers.)

stem.en: p-Dichlorobenzene has a much higher melting point than its ortho and meta isomers because:

explanation.en: The para isomer is symmetrical and fits closely into the crystal lattice, so more energy is needed to melt it. Its dipole moment is actually zero; all three isomers have the same molar mass, and none of them hydrogen-bonds.

options.en: It has the largest dipole moment
It is symmetrical and packs better in the crystal lattice
It has the highest molar mass

stem.en: The correct order of reactivity towards SN2 substitution is:

explanation.en: In SN2 the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the leaving group through a crowded five-coordinate transition state. Each extra alkyl group adds steric hindrance, so methyl > 1° > 2° > 3°. The reverse order is the SN1 order (carbocation stability).

stem.en: Which compound undergoes SN1 hydrolysis the fastest?

explanation.en: The rate-determining step is ionisation to a carbocation. (C₆H₅)₂CH⁺ is stabilised by resonance with two benzene rings, more than the benzyl cation (one ring), which in turn is far more stable than the isopropyl and ethyl cations.

stem.en: (R)-2-Bromobutane reacts with aqueous NaOH by the SN2 mechanism. The product is:

explanation.en: SN2 inverts the configuration (Walden inversion). In the reactant the priorities are Br > C₂H₅ > CH₃ > H; in the product OH > C₂H₅ > CH₃ > H. OH takes the place of Br in priority but sits on the opposite side, so the R label becomes S. A racemic mixture is the SN1 outcome, and but-2-ene would come from elimination with alcoholic KOH.

stem.en: Alkyl halides give alkyl cyanides (R–CN) with KCN but isocyanides (R–NC) with AgCN. The reason is:

explanation.en: CN⁻ is ambident: it can attack through C or N. KCN is ionic and supplies free CN⁻, which attacks through carbon (C–C bond is stronger), giving R–CN. AgCN is largely covalent (Ag–C≡N); carbon is tied up with silver, so nitrogen's lone pair attacks, giving R–NC. CN⁻ has lone pairs on both atoms.

options.en: KCN is covalent and AgCN is ionic
The cyanide ion has a lone pair only on nitrogen
Silver ions react with nitriles to form isocyanides
KCN is ionic, so the more nucleophilic carbon attacks; AgCN is mainly covalent, so only the nitrogen lone pair is free to attack

stem.en: Match the reagent (reacting with R–X) with the main product. (a) KCN (b) AgCN (c) KNO₂ (d) AgNO₂; (i) R–NC (ii) R–NO₂ (iii) R–CN (iv) R–O–N=O

explanation.en: Ionic salts supply the free ambident anion: CN⁻ from KCN attacks through C (giving the nitrile), and NO₂⁻ from KNO₂ attacks through O (giving the alkyl nitrite). The silver salts are largely covalent, so the atom bonded to Ag is tied up and the other end attacks: AgCN gives the isocyanide (N attacks) and AgNO₂ gives the nitroalkane (N attacks).

stem.en: Propene reacts with HBr in the presence of benzoyl peroxide. The major product is:

explanation.en: With peroxide, HBr adds by a free-radical chain (Kharasch / peroxide effect): Br• adds to the terminal carbon to give the more stable secondary radical, then H is taken from HBr. The result is anti-Markovnikov 1-bromopropane. Without peroxide, Markovnikov addition gives 2-bromopropane. The peroxide effect is not seen with HCl or HI.

stem.en: Assertion (A): Chlorobenzene is far less reactive than chloromethane towards nucleophilic substitution. Reason (R): Due to resonance, the C–Cl bond in chlorobenzene acquires partial double-bond character.

explanation.en: A Cl lone pair delocalises into the ring, giving the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character; it is shorter (169 pm against 177 pm in CH₃Cl) and harder to break. Other factors (sp² carbon, unstable phenyl cation, electron-rich ring repelling the nucleophile) add to it, but R is the standard and correct explanation.

options.en: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

stem.en: The correct order of ease of hydrolysis (by aqueous NaOH) of the following is:

explanation.en: Nitro groups at ortho and para positions withdraw electrons and delocalise the negative charge of the Meisenheimer intermediate. More such groups mean milder conditions: chlorobenzene needs 623 K and 300 atm, 4-nitro about 443 K, 2,4-dinitro about 368 K, and 2,4,6-trinitro reacts with warm water (≈ 323 K).

options.en: All four react at the same rate

stem.en: Chlorobenzene and chloromethane are treated together with sodium in dry ether. The cross-coupled product is:

explanation.en: Wurtz–Fittig reaction: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl} + \text{CH}_3\text{Cl} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3 + 2\text{NaCl}$. Biphenyl (Fittig) and ethane (Wurtz) form only as side products from like–like coupling.

stem.en: How many moles of methane are produced when 1 mole of 2-aminoethanol (HO–CH₂–CH₂–NH₂) reacts with excess CH₃MgBr? (in mol)

explanation.en: CH₃MgBr removes every 'active' hydrogen (on O, N, S or terminal alkyne C) as CH₄. 2-Aminoethanol has one O–H and two N–H, so 3 mol CH₄. The C–H bonds of CH₂ are not acidic enough.

stem.en: Which halomethane has the highest dipole moment?

explanation.en: Dipole moments: CH₃Cl 1.860 D, CH₃F 1.847 D, CH₃Br 1.830 D, CH₃I 1.636 D. F is the most electronegative, but the C–F bond is so short that the charge × distance product is slightly smaller than for C–Cl. Picking CH₃F is the classic trap.

stem.en: The correct order of density of the following liquids is:

explanation.en: Density rises with the number and mass of halogen atoms: CH₂Cl₂ (≈ 1.34 g cm⁻³) < CHCl₃ (≈ 1.49) < CCl₄ (≈ 1.59).

stem.en: Statement I: In chlorobenzene, chlorine deactivates the ring towards electrophilic substitution. Statement II: Chlorine directs incoming electrophiles to the ortho and para positions.

explanation.en: Cl withdraws electrons inductively (−I), which outweighs its resonance donation (+R), so the ring is less reactive than benzene. But +R raises electron density specifically at ortho and para, and it stabilises the σ-complexes for o/p attack, so it is an o/p director. Both statements are correct.

options.en: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect

stem.en: A primary alkyl bromide reacts with OH⁻ by the SN2 mechanism. If the concentrations of both the alkyl bromide and OH⁻ are doubled, by what factor does the initial rate increase?

explanation.en: Rate $= k[\text{RBr}][\text{OH}^-]$. Doubling both gives $2 \times 2 = 4$ times the rate. For an SN1 reaction (rate $= k[\text{RBr}]$) the same change would only double the rate.

stem.en: 2-Bromobutane is heated with alcoholic KOH. How many different alkenes (including stereoisomers) can form?

explanation.en: Loss of H from C-1 gives but-1-ene; loss of H from C-3 gives but-2-ene, which exists as cis and trans isomers. Total 3 (trans-but-2-ene is the major product). Answering 2 forgets the geometrical isomers.

stem.en: How many of the following compounds are chiral? 2-chlorobutane, 1-chlorobutane, 2-chloro-2-methylbutane, 3-chloropentane, 2-bromo-3-methylbutane, 1-chloro-2-methylbutane

explanation.en: Chiral: 2-chlorobutane (C-2: H, Cl, CH₃, C₂H₅); 2-bromo-3-methylbutane (C-2: H, Br, CH₃, CH(CH₃)₂); 1-chloro-2-methylbutane (C-2: H, CH₃, C₂H₅, CH₂Cl). Achiral: 1-chlorobutane (no stereocentre), 2-chloro-2-methylbutane (two CH₃ on C-2) and 3-chloropentane (two C₂H₅ on C-3). Total 3.

stem.en: Optically active 3-bromo-3-methylhexane is hydrolysed in aqueous acetone (SN1 conditions). The product 3-methylhexan-3-ol is obtained:

explanation.en: The tertiary bromide ionises to a planar carbocation, which water can attack from either face. Both enantiomers form, so the product is largely racemic (often with slight excess of inversion because the departing Br⁻ briefly shields one face). Complete inversion is the SN2 outcome; meso needs two stereocentres.

stem.en: Which chloride is the most reactive towards SN1 substitution?

explanation.en: Allyl chloride ionises to the resonance-stabilised allyl cation (CH₂=CH–CH₂⁺ ↔ ⁺CH₂–CH=CH₂), so it reacts readily. n-Propyl chloride gives an unstable primary cation. Vinyl chloride and chlorobenzene have a C–Cl bond with partial double-bond character on an sp² carbon and are very unreactive.

stem.en: For a given alkyl group, the order of reactivity of alkyl halides in nucleophilic substitution is:

explanation.en: The C–X bond enthalpy falls from C–F to C–I and the halide ion becomes a weaker base (better leaving group), so R–I reacts fastest and R–F slowest. The order of bond polarity is the opposite, which is why the reversed option is tempting.

stem.en: 2-Methylbutane is monochlorinated in light. How many monochloro products are possible, counting stereoisomers separately?

explanation.en: There are four kinds of H in (CH₃)₂CH–CH₂–CH₃. 1-Chloro-2-methylbutane (C-2 becomes chiral: 2 enantiomers); 2-chloro-2-methylbutane (achiral: 1); 2-chloro-3-methylbutane (C-2 chiral: 2); 1-chloro-3-methylbutane (achiral: 1). Total 4 structural isomers and 6 stereoisomeric products.

stem.en: How many structural isomers of C₅H₁₁Br are primary alkyl bromides?

explanation.en: 1-Bromopentane; 1-bromo-2-methylbutane; 1-bromo-3-methylbutane; 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentyl bromide). Total 4. (The other four C₅H₁₁Br isomers are 2-bromopentane, 3-bromopentane, 2-bromo-3-methylbutane (secondary) and 2-bromo-2-methylbutane (tertiary).)

stem.en: Which of the following statements about the SN2 mechanism is/are correct?

explanation.en: SN2 is concerted: the bond to the nucleophile forms as the C–X bond breaks, so rate $= k[\text{RX}][\text{Nu}^-]$ (A) and back-side attack inverts the configuration (B). Polar aprotic solvents do not solvate the nucleophile strongly, leaving it reactive (D). A carbocation intermediate is the hallmark of SN1, so C is wrong.

options.en: It occurs in a single step and is second order overall
It proceeds with inversion of configuration at the carbon attacked
It is favoured by polar aprotic solvents such as acetone or DMSO

stem.en: Which of the following statements about the SN1 mechanism is/are correct?

explanation.en: The slow step is ionisation of R–X alone, so rate $= k[\text{RX}]$ (B). A free carbocation can undergo hydride or methyl shifts (C). The benzyl cation is resonance-stabilised whereas the ethyl cation is not (D). The planar carbocation is attacked on both faces, giving racemisation, not complete inversion (A is wrong).

options.en: It proceeds with complete inversion of configuration
Its rate does not depend on the concentration of the nucleophile
Rearrangement of the carbon skeleton is possible
Benzyl chloride reacts faster than ethyl chloride by this mechanism

stem.en: Which of the following statements about chlorobenzene is/are correct?

explanation.en: Partial double-bond character and sp² carbon make the C–Cl bond shorter (≈ 169 pm vs 177 pm) (A). Without activating groups, displacement of Cl needs drastic conditions (B). Fittig reaction: 2C₆H₅Cl + 2Na → C₆H₅–C₆H₅ + 2NaCl (C). Chlorine is deactivating (−I > +R), so D is wrong even though it is o/p directing.

options.en: Its C–Cl bond is shorter than the C–Cl bond in chloromethane
It is converted to phenol by aqueous NaOH at about 623 K and 300 atm (Dow process)
Heating it with sodium in dry ether gives biphenyl
The chlorine atom activates the ring towards electrophilic substitution

stem.en: In which of the following reactions of alkyl halides is a new C–C bond formed?

explanation.en: Wurtz coupling joins two alkyl groups (R–R) (B), and cyanide attacks through carbon to give R–C≡N (C), which adds one carbon to the chain. Finkelstein (A) and Swarts (D) only exchange one halogen for another.

stem.en: Which of the following statements about polyhalogen compounds is/are correct?

explanation.en: DDT is stable, poorly metabolised and fat-soluble, so it accumulates along food chains (B). CHCl₃ + O₂ (light) gives COCl₂ (C). CCl₄ reaching the upper atmosphere releases Cl atoms that destroy ozone (D). Freons were chosen because they are unreactive, non-toxic and non-corrosive, so A is wrong.

options.en: Freons are highly reactive and toxic, which is why they were used as refrigerants
DDT is not biodegradable and accumulates in the fatty tissue of animals
Chloroform is slowly oxidised by air in light to phosgene
Release of CCl₄ into the air contributes to depletion of the ozone layer

stem.en: Propene is treated with HBr in the presence of peroxide to give A. A is heated with alcoholic KOH to give B. B is treated with HBr (no peroxide) to give C. C is:

explanation.en: A = 1-bromopropane (anti-Markovnikov, peroxide effect). Dehydrobromination of A with alcoholic KOH gives B = propene. Ordinary (ionic) addition of HBr to propene follows Markovnikov's rule: C = 2-bromopropane. The sequence is a way to move Br from C-1 to C-2.

stem.en: Neopentyl bromide, (CH₃)₃C–CH₂Br, is heated in aqueous ethanol with Ag⁺ (forcing SN1 conditions). The main substitution product is:

explanation.en: Ionisation would give the very unstable primary cation (CH₃)₃C–CH₂⁺, which immediately undergoes a 1,2-methyl shift to the tertiary cation (CH₃)₂C⁺–CH₂CH₃. Water attacks that cation to give 2-methylbutan-2-ol. 2,2-Dimethylpropan-1-ol would need direct substitution without rearrangement, which SN2 cannot achieve here because of extreme steric hindrance.

stem.en: The correct order of SN2 rate with I⁻ in acetone is:

explanation.en: n-Propyl bromide is an unhindered primary halide and reacts fastest. Isopropyl bromide is secondary and slower. Neopentyl bromide is primary, but the bulky tert-butyl group next to the reacting carbon blocks back-side attack so completely that it is roughly 10⁵ times slower than ethyl bromide, slower even than the secondary halide. Ranking by '1° > 2°' alone gives the wrong fourth option.

stem.en: 3-Chlorobut-1-ene, CH₂=CH–CHCl–CH₃, is hydrolysed under SN1 conditions. The product is:

explanation.en: Ionisation gives an allylic cation with positive charge shared between C-1 and C-3: CH₂=CH–CH⁺–CH₃ ↔ ⁺CH₂–CH=CH–CH₃. Water attacks either end, giving but-3-en-2-ol and the rearranged but-2-en-1-ol (allylic rearrangement). Butan-2-ol would need the double bond to be reduced; but-1-en-1-ol is an unstable enol.

options.en: A mixture of but-3-en-2-ol and but-2-en-1-ol
